nameStory: The Eastern American Platterful gets its name from its impressively large, flat cap that can reach dinner plate proportions when fully mature. The word 'platterful' captures both the size and the slightly dished shape of older specimens, which look like they could hold a generous serving of food.
description: The Eastern American Platterful is a hefty mushroom that commands attention with its broad, tan to brown cap and sturdy white stem. This impressive fungus can grow quite large, with caps reaching 4-8 inches across and stems up to 6 inches tall. It has closely spaced white gills underneath and often grows in small clusters from buried wood or roots. The overall appearance is robust and meaty, making it one of the more substantial mushrooms you'll encounter in New England forests.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Large and flat to slightly depressed, tan to brown with a smooth, dry surface that feels like soft leather. Often has subtle radial streaks and may crack slightly in dry weather.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: White to cream colored, closely spaced, and attached to the stem. They feel firm to the touch and don't bruise when gently pressed.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick, white, and often swollen at the base with a fibrous, slightly fuzzy texture. May have root-like extensions (rhizomorphs) extending into the soil.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: White to pale cream when collected on dark paper overnight.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant and mild, sometimes described as slightly floury or yeasty, especially when crushed.

habitat: Found in mixed hardwood and coniferous forests throughout New England, typically growing from buried wood, roots, or rich organic soil. Prefers well-drained areas near oak, maple, and pine trees at elevations from sea level to mid-mountains. Often appears along woodland trails and in forest clearings where there's partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen, though small buttons may occasionally emerge during warm, wet periods in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak season begins in mid to late summer, especially after periods of steady rain. Look for young specimens with tightly curved cap edges.
seasonality.fall: Most abundant during early to mid-fall when temperatures are mild and moisture is consistent. Mature specimens show their full platter-like shape now.
seasonality.winter: Disappears completely in New England winters, leaving no visible traces above ground.

funFact: This mushroom can live underground for years through an extensive network of root-like fungal threads called rhizomorphs that can stretch over 30 feet through the soil, suddenly producing clusters of mushrooms when conditions are just right.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with large specimens of Honey Mushrooms, but Platterful mushrooms lack the dark scales on the cap and don't grow in the dense, overlapping clusters typical of Honey Mushrooms. Remember: Platterful = smooth cap, Honey = scaly cap.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its impressive size and meaty appearance, there's limited information about this mushroom's edibility, and some related species can cause digestive upset. The genus name Megacollybia literally means 'giant Collybia,' referring to its supersized version of the smaller, more common Collybia mushrooms.
compareHints: As the only Megacollybia species commonly found in New England, it's most similar to large Collybia species, but dwarfs them in size and has a much more robust stem structure. Unlike the smaller Collybia mushrooms that have thin, hollow stems, the Platterful's stem is thick and solid with distinctive root-like extensions.
